title: Type Aliases
summary: A type alias gives a reusable name to a type.

subtopics.title: Create a name
subtopics.explanation: Use `type Name = ...` to give a type a readable name. For example, `type UserId = string` labels a value as an ID for people reading the code. It is like naming a drawer. This simple alias does not create a distinct runtime type from `string`. For example, use a union alias for a request state with loading, success, and error cases.

subtopics.title: Allowed choices
subtopics.explanation: A union type lists values that are allowed alternatives, such as `"loading" | "ready" | "error"`. It is like a status sign with three possible states. TypeScript can check that code handles the choices. Unions are useful for state and configuration values with a known set of options. For example, name a shared product shape once instead of repeating it in every function.

subtopics.title: Object shapes
subtopics.explanation: A type alias can name an object shape, such as `{ name: string; active: boolean }`, or a function signature. It is like labeling a reusable form. Use it when several parts of a program should agree on what data looks like, and keep the name tied to its role. For example, use a function type when several callbacks share the same input and output contract.

subtopics.title: Runtime behavior
subtopics.explanation: Type aliases are erased from the emitted JavaScript. They do not validate incoming JSON or create constructors by themselves. It is like a label written in a blueprint that is not attached to the delivered object. Use runtime checks when an application must verify data while it runs. For example, remember a type alias does not create a runtime constructor.

subtopics.title: Useful names
subtopics.explanation: Choose names that explain what a value represents, such as `SearchResult` or `ThemeMode`. A name like `Thing` gives little guidance. It is like labeling a drawer by its contents. Clear names make editor hints and error messages more useful to the whole team. For example, use a branded pattern only when plain strings must not be mixed accidentally.

foundations.overview: A type alias gives a useful name to a type expression. It can describe a union of choices, an object shape, or a function signature. Think of it like giving a long instruction a short label. Type aliases exist for TypeScript’s checks and are removed when JavaScript runs, so they do not create runtime values or validation.
foundations.whyItMatters: Aliases give names to complex shapes and allowed choices. Good names make function signatures easier to read, while over-general aliases can couple unrelated features.
foundations.browserPerspective: Type aliases are purely compile-time. They're erased during compilation, so the emitted JavaScript contains no trace of them and they add zero runtime cost.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Naming React prop types (type Props = {...}), API response shapes, status unions (type Status = 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'), reusable callback signatures, and generic helpers like Nullable<T> or ApiResponse<T>.
foundations.businessImpact: Reusable, named types reduce duplication and drift between definitions, lowering the chance of mismatched shapes causing bugs in features that share data.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Defining a shape once and referencing it everywhere means a change is made in one place and type-checked across all usages, easing refactors.
foundations.performanceImpact: None at runtime (erased). Very large unions or deeply nested alias compositions can slow the type-checker/editor, so keep composed aliases reasonable.
commonUseCases: Typing React props and config objects
Generic helpers like Nullable<T> or ApiResponse<T>
Limit a value to a small set of string states.
Share a callback contract across components.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A type alias creates a brand-new, distinct type.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's just a name for an existing type; aliased primitives are structurally identical and interchangeable with the underlying type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: type aliases and interfaces are completely interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only interfaces support declaration merging; only type aliases can name unions, tuples, primitives, and function types directly. They overlap mainly for object shapes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A type alias creates a new distinct runtime value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Aliases are erased and often remain structurally compatible with their underlying type.

commonMisconceptions.myth: One alias should describe every field in an application.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Focused names keep contracts understandable and limit unnecessary coupling.

config.intro: Trace type Status = 'active' | 'archived' from definition to reuse.

steps.name: Define the alias
steps.detail: type Status = 'active' | 'archived' names a union of two string literals.

steps.name: Reference by name
steps.detail: Use Status anywhere a variable or parameter should hold one of those values.

steps.name: Compiler substitutes
steps.detail: TypeScript treats Status as 'active' | 'archived' wherever it appears.

steps.name: Check usage
steps.detail: Assigning 'deleted' to a Status is a compile error — it's not in the union.

steps.name: Erase on emit
steps.detail: The alias disappears at compile time; the emitted JavaScript has no Status type.

codeLab.title: Name a callback type with an alias
codeLab.instructions: Define a type alias Callback for a function that takes a string message and returns void. Then use it to type the onLog parameter of run.
hints: Use the type keyword with a function signature: (message: string) => void.
Annotate the onLog parameter with your Callback alias.

keyTakeaways: A union type lists values that are allowed alternatives, such as `"loading" | "ready" | "error"`.
A type alias can name an object shape, such as `{ name: string; active: boolean }`, or a function signature.
Type aliases are erased from the emitted JavaScript.
Choose names that explain what a value represents, such as `SearchResult` or `ThemeMode`.
